item.title: Study Hard, Get a Career, Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
item.description:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

In many places around the world, that system has proved to be remarkably effective, in large part because education has translated relatively straightforwardly into economic mobility.

But increasingly, many who work hard at higher education, often going into debt and sacrificing years of earnings potential to do so, are finding that the rewards are not there at the end. Instead of expected winnings, many young people are greeted with a life of economic struggle.

This discontent is affecting politics elsewhere as well. In the United States, data from The New York Times showed that 70 percent of voters under 30 in the recent midterm elections cast their ballots for Democrats, who tapped educated young people’s widespread frustration over being saddled with debt and stuck in low-paid, dead-end jobs.

In Serbia, student protests grew into a political movement that ousted Aleksandar Vucic, the country’s longtime nationalist strongman, in an election last month. And young people across Europe are set to walk out on Nov. 20 in a general strike that could disrupt schools and businesses throughout the continent.

An even bigger threat looms on the horizon, one that could upend the bargain everywhere: A.I. promises to dramatically restructure, or perhaps sever completely, the relationship between education and well-paid work.

That has the potential to further challenge not only the distribution of economic rewards, but the political bargain on which modern societies have been built.

Historically, such moments have been explosive — even revolutionary.

The version of the meritocratic bargain we see today, with university education as a primary filter for middle-class careers, is a relatively recent construct, and not to be taken for granted.

Britain didn’t introduce universal, free secondary education until 1944. In the United States, college was largely the province of the privileged few until the G.I. Bill opened access to veterans after World War II. Around the same time, the SAT created the first nationally standardized benchmark for admissions.

In countries whose economies developed later, the bargain took even longer to take shape. In India, the national college entrance exam was not introduced until the 1960s. In China, there is a long history of using meritocratic exams to select civil servants and other elites, but that system was disrupted by 20th-century reforms and the Cultural Revolution. The modern system was ushered in by Deng Xiaoping. In 1977 he re-established the national “gaokao” exam system as part of a post-Cultural Revolution rebuilding process. In the late 1990s, further reforms radically expanded university access.

For individuals, this access to education promised more money, more status or both. But for governments, it also offered political stability — a way to convince people to buy into society as currently structured, by promising the potential for advancement to the underprivileged without ousting those who had wealth and power already.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Research has shown that the prospect of upward mobility — sometimes abbreviated as POUM — can make the poor less likely to demand redistribution. In China, merit-based selection for civil service jobs made people more willing to tolerate inequality, Hanzhang Liu, a political scientist at Florida State University, has found.

When people believed the system was meritocratic, they were more likely to attribute their failures to their own poor abilities, or to the high quality of the competition, she said. But when they did not believe so, those who lost out on jobs were more likely to consider the system rigged.

Still, education-based meritocracy puts significant burdens on the young people working to advance, and on their families. In India, students often go into debt and spend years of grueling study to try to win spots at the most prestigious engineering and medical programs.

In South Korea, national tests have generated an entire industry of cram schools known as hagwons, where students toil for hours each day on top of their regular schoolwork. In the United States, networks of charter schools like KIPP popularized the idea that for poor, ambitious kids, “college starts in kindergarten.” And when actual college starts, American students can easily take on six-figure debts for their degrees.

Just as the meritocratic bargain can be a source of social cohesion, a breakdown can become a trigger for social explosion.

In 1905, China abolished the national civil service exam that had for 1,300 years been a major way to recruit elites, including government bureaucrats. That move came as a shock to the people who had invested in years of education, hoping to earn a privileged position in society.

Those shattered expectations contributed to the revolutionary uprisings that eventually overthrew the imperial dynasty in 1911, according to the economists Ying Bai, at the University of Hong Kong, and Ruixue Jia, at the University of California, San Diego.

In an influential 2016 paper, they found that frustrated commoners who had hoped to become elites via the exam were especially likely to join the revolution. Disillusioned scholars flocked to revolutionary organizations in search of alternative routes to advancement, and became a major force behind the revolt.

That is not to say that France’s unrest signals the imminent return of the guillotine. But the recent protests there, and in other European countries like Italy and Spain, were fueled, in part, by the sense that the old order was enriching itself at the expense of providing opportunities for young people.

Much the same can be said of the student protest movement that led to the election defeat of Mr. Vucic in Serbia, where angry young people felt that meritocratic opportunity had been crowded out by corruption.

Protests can be a blunt instrument. But data show that the demonstrators have a point. In Europe, high unemployment rates for young people, paired with skyrocketing costs of living, have put the traditional milestones of independent adulthood out of reach for many.

Even in countries with healthier economies, there are signs that the breakdown of the meritocratic bargain is already having political consequences. In India, economic growth has been stronger, but it has not created enough jobs to keep up with the expansion of higher education.

In the United States, the emphasis on higher education as a sorting mechanism has led to people pouring tens of thousands of dollars into degrees that no longer necessarily confer economic advancement but still charge as if they do. Discontent has fueled the rise of political movements like the Democratic Socialists of America and efforts to unionize the work forces of companies like Starbucks and Amazon, Noam Scheiber, a Times labor reporter, writes in his new book, “Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class.”

But the biggest blow to the meritocratic bargain may be yet to come, as many fear that A.I. could do for knowledge work what a meteor strike once did for the dinosaurs.

A.I.’s arrival has already wiped out some entry-level technical jobs. In the United States, young coders are finding themselves working at Chipotle rather than starting the highly paid tech careers they had expected.

Even if A.I. does not eliminate professionals like lawyers, scientists and doctors, it may radically reshape those fields — and perhaps slash the salaries that come with them.

Some professions may adapt by making greater use of A.I. tools, even as other careers see their pay and numbers collapse. With time, new educational structures may also develop to match skills and meritocratic selection to the demands of a new economy.

But such profound economic change is by its very nature disruptive. In the meantime, it is likely to sow even more confusion about how young people can set themselves up for success, or prevent themselves from sliding down the economic ladder.

item.title: A Grizzly Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules Banff Park, and Draws a Crowd
item.description:
To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.

He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.

Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.

But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

Among those concerned about the cost of celebrity is Paul Kalra, a gas station owner and nature photographer who drew attention to the bear more than 20 years ago with photos in a local newspaper and is widely credited with naming him.

“Give him a break,” Mr. Kalra said, sitting at a table at the restaurant in his service station in Dead Man’s Flats. “Even the movie stars that are most famous, they go incognito with sunglasses when they go to have a burger, you know? I want same thing for the Boss.”

About 75 grizzly bears roam the mountains, rivers and valleys of Banff National Park’s 6,641 square kilometers. How the Boss came to stand out is a matter of geography as much as his size and legends. His home turf overlaps with the park’s main tourist gateway.

Grizzlies can, of course, be dangerous. This month conservation officers in British Columbia killed a female grizzly and her three cubs after DNA connected them to a fatal attack on a women and her daughter.

But although the Boss strolled into Canmore, a former coal mining town just east of the park three years ago, apparently looking for crab apples, David Laskin, a Parks Canada wildlife ecologist said the danger that most grizzlies pose is overstated.

“A lot of people rob themselves of enjoyable experiences in the wilderness because they’re scared of bears,” he said at a park picnic table festooned with signs warning against feeding animals. “Bears need to be respected. Getting close to a bear: There’s a risk for you but also for the bear especially. We don’t want to put bears in a situation where they have to defend themselves.”

The Boss has eaten other bears, but he and all of Banff’s grizzlies are largely vegetarians, Dr. Laskin said. Berries, roots and other plant materials make up about 90 percent of their diet. Maintaining 700 pounds on a berry-heavy diet forces grizzlies to range widely and eat vigorously. The Boss can put away about 200,000 buffaloberries a day, Dr. Laskin said. When he wore a tracking collar for most of 2012, he traveled about 1,400 kilometers in search of food.

“They’re actually surprisingly delicate in how they pull berries from shrubs, from branches,” he said. “They’ll use their claws and they’ll just pull a branch to their mouths and just kind of nibble off the berries”

Locals are quick to volunteer Boss stories. Bill Hunt, the former natural resources conservation manager at Banff, had an encounter about three years ago as he was packing to move from his Canmore house.

“I was packing up the U-Haul and he came walking right up the street past my house, probably 12 feet away,” Mr. Hunt said. “That’s why he got that name. He could have gone around, he could have gone down the power line, 20 feet below the house. But he came right down the middle of the road — big white claws hanging over the front.”

Mr. Kalra won’t profit off the Boss by selling photos of the bear, but he displays some at his service station. Mr. Kalra, who was born in India and moved to moved to Canmore in 1989, said that, like Mr. Hunt, he has always been struck by the bear’s indifference toward humans.

“The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Mr. Kalra said. “He has never done any harm to anyone. And that means more to me than anything else.”

Under the park’s bear management plan, the Boss is “habituated,” a category for bears that don’t really care about people as long as they are left alone.

That said, when the park’s network of trail cams, sightings and paw prints suggests that he’s headed toward Banff, Canmore or campgrounds, park workers gently shoo him in another direction while clearing visitors from his path. (It’s unclear if plans to eliminate 500 jobs at Parks Canada will affect that program.)

Despite the large influx of visitors into Banff, serious bear incidents remain rare, Mr. Hunt said. They generally involve “wary” bears, the vast majority of the population, in remote parts of the park.

“When you’re encountering a wary bear that hadn’t seen a person in three months, both sides are scared and terrified, and the bigger animal wins,” Mr. Hunt said. “It’s often just a quick swat and then they realize what they’ve encountered and they take off.”

But the most worrisome bears, Mr. Hunt said, are those that decide that exploiting human activity — from garbage to bird feeders and fruit trees — beats looking for berries.

“It’s very subtle, but it’s a very big change,” Mr. Hunt said. “That is when bears become dangerous.”

In addition to the signs ordering park visitors not to feed animals, Canmore and Banff have strict rules around garbage and programs to replace fruit trees.

Now in his mid-20s, the Boss is getting old for a bear, prompting speculation about whether he will emerge from hibernation in the spring.

Earlier this year, Dr. Laskin got up close with him. The Boss was found in a trap set for another study bear. “We thought he was too smart for that,” he said. The Boss was sedated, examined and fitted for a collar that soon fell off, most likely in a fight.

Grizzlies typically peak physically at about 10 and then gradually shrink, but Dr. Laskin said that there’s no sign of that in the Boss.

His teeth, however, are “worn, but that’s not unusual for a bear his age.”

His odor? “Not a good smell.”

When asked about the Boss’s fur, Dr. Laskin demurred at first.

“I shouldn’t make any comments about the tactile characteristics of grizzly bears,” he said, apparently concerned that some visitors might treat the park as a petting zoo.

Then he relented.

“Their name comes from the characteristics of their fur, where you have a soft coat with guard hairs that extend beyond that coat,” he said. “They’re a bit lighter than the rest of the coat, and it gives that grizzled appearance. And, yeah, they’re soft.”

item.title: Too Many Chips in One Basket?
item.description:
A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.

Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”

But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.

Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”

The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

Just as there is no clear successor to Huang at Nvidia — as my colleagues have written, he actively avoided grooming one — there is currently no real substitute for Nvidia itself. It is arguably the most important company in the most important industry in the world. It’s also vital to the U.S. economy and American national security.

Which raises the question: With the stakes this high, why were so many chips in one basket? Why isn’t there another Nvidia?

A big head start

It’s hard to overstate Nvidia’s importance.

The company controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. When you talk to, for example, ChatGPT, its computer chips in A.I. data centers are what make it talk back.

Outside the United States? More Nvidia chips. Even Chinese labs, which are barred from buying the most advanced models, often use earlier versions.

Competition? It has very little. Tech giants like Google and Amazon have made chips that have saved them some money and reduced their dependence on Nvidia. A longtime rival, Advanced Micro Devices, has also grabbed a share of the market, as have some start-ups. But companies keep coming back for Nvidia chips.

I spoke to Don Clark, who has been covering chips for over four decades, including for The New York Times. He told me that the story of Nvidia’s stunning dominance is largely thanks to the savvy and the foresight of … Jensen Huang.

Huang spotted the potential of A.I. early on, and pivoted a decade before any other chip makers did. That head start allowed Nvidia to build up layers of widely used software and specialized models needed for A.I., which require Nvidia chips to run.

And Nvidia isn’t just the world’s dominant chip maker. It is also what some have called the “central bank of A.I.” It has helped to finance the industry’s growth through a series of complex deals with its customers and suppliers — and it’s not clear any other company is ready to step in and fill that gap.

With great power comes great exposure

Nvidia has long been a crucial American asset. Its chips have given the United States a strategic advantage over China. The company has allowed the U.S. to exercise control — to some degree, anyway — over who has access to these chips and, specifically, to prevent China from obtaining its most advanced models. To use a term that’s become increasingly important, Nvidia is a choke point.

Nvidia isn’t the only choke point in A.I.; the industry is replete with them. Nvidia designs the chips, which are then manufactured by one Taiwan-based company, TSMC. TSMC, in turn, depends on manufacturing tools produced by one Dutch company, ASML.

I spoke to Edward Fishman, who recently wrote a book called “Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare.” He described a manufacturing ecosystem of “exquisite” complexity with “so many different sub-components that even the sub-components themselves can become their own choke points.”

But the Huang affair has crystallized something important. Choke points offer strategic advantages; they can also become vulnerabilities.

For China, Fishman said, compromising Nvidia could “weaken the leverage of the U.S. in this industry, and maybe even have a macro impact on the U.S. economy.”

Roughly half of economic growth in the U.S. last year was powered by the A.I. boom. Roughly a third of America’s total stock market value comes from big A.I. companies. And even after its recent decline, Nvidia still accounts for roughly a quarter of the value of those A.I. stocks.

Nvidia’s dominant position is not going to disappear overnight. Its next three years of chip production are already largely under contract and won’t be affected much by Huang’s departure, Don said. But further down the line, his absence might be felt more. The company is also likely to continue facing scrutiny from Congress, which is still pushing for answers, despite Huang’s departure, and could even face legal risks.

Nvidia will get another C.E.O., Don said. An interim one is in place already. But “there won’t be another Jensen Huang,” he added. “It’s just like there’s not another Steve Jobs. He’s one of a kind.”

Which is why things suddenly feel so wobbly.

Huang’s resignation shocked people in Taiwan, his birthplace, where he is called “the people’s dad.”

Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain yesterday for the second time in days. The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said that Iranian forces had targeted a radar system at a Bahraini air base.

The attack occurred just as the U.S. appeared to have stepped back from efforts to reach a peace deal with Iran. The U.S. military said it shot down two drones fired by Iran toward Bahrain on Friday. The attacks were the first to target Bahrain in about two months.

Related: Officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a number of cyberattacks and attempted attacks across Europe.

The wreck of Yamamoto’s Mitsubishi G4M1 — a Betty, as that type of plane was code-named by the Allies during World War II — has remained deep in the jungle for some 80 years. item.title: Powerful ’80s Mexican Drug Lord Dies as a Prisoner
item.description:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a notorious Mexican drug lord who helped build the foundations of the modern drug trade, died a prisoner at the age of 80 on Sunday, according to the Mexican authorities.

Mr. Félix Gallardo became internationally known in the 1980s after the United States Drug Enforcement Administration accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of an undercover agent, Enrique (Kiki) Salazar Camarena.

On Friday, after decades behind bars, Mr. Félix Gallardo was transferred from the Puente Grande prison complex to a private hospital in Guadalajara after a medical emergency, according to the Jalisco state secretary of public security. He died around 2 p.m. Sunday of multiple organ failure, the agency said in a statement, citing medical personnel who treated him.

A small religious ceremony will be held at the hospital in the presence of his relatives, according to Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesman for the Secretary of Public Security of Jalisco state.

When Mr. Félix Gallardo was arrested in 1989, he was described by the Mexican attorney general, Enrique Alvarez del Castillo, as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”

Before founding the Guadalajara Cartel, he had worked as a police officer and had served as a bodyguard to Sinaloa’s governor — connections that helped him and his partners transform the Mexican drug trade in the 1970s and 1980s.

Joaquín Guzmán Loera — the infamous Mexican drug kingpin known as El Chapo who helped run the Sinaloa Cartel before his arrest in 2014 — got his start in the business working as an air logistics expert for Mr. Félix Gallardo.

It was the murder of the undercover agent that led the American authorities to seek the capture of Mr. Félix Gallardo and his associates. At the time of his death in 1985, Mr. Salazar Camarena had been “extremely close to unlocking a multi-billion-dollar drug pipeline,” according to the agency.

The agent’s body, along with that of a pilot who worked for him and had been kidnapped separately, was found a month after he disappeared. A major manhunt followed — and eventually an intensification of the war on drugs.

The killing strained relations between Mexico and the United States, as Washington demanded that the Mexican authorities bring those responsible to justice. The case has inspired numerous books, films and television series, including Netflix’s “Narcos: Mexico.”

When the agent was killed, American officials said they believed Mr. Félix Gallardo was involved along with two other drug-trafficking figures, Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, who had been arrested and charged.

After his arrest in 1989, Mr. Félix Gallardo denied having had a hand in the killing or playing any role in drug trafficking. But in the end, he was sentenced to 40 years in prison in connection with drug trafficking, bribery and corruption charges. In 2017, he was also sentenced to 37 years in prison in connection with the killing of the American agent.

At the time of his arrest, Mr. Félix Gallardo had been wanted by the Mexican and American authorities for more than a decade. During that period, he had continued to operate freely in Mexico with the protection of police and other government officials.

item.title: American Global Health Aid Isn’t Dead. It’s Changing.
item.description:
Americans might have assumed that their country was out of the business of promoting global health. On his first day in office, President Trump announced the United States’ withdrawal from the World Health Organization and abruptly “paused” foreign aid. Over the following weeks, Elon Musk took a chain saw to the U.S. Agency for International Development.

In the wake of these actions, reporters documented shortages of tuberculosis, malaria and H.I.V. drugs, widespread clinic closures and the abandonment of patients enrolled in medical trials. Many programs never resumed, and researchers predicted that hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths would occur in the first year alone. Assessing whether this came true is complicated by the fact that programs tracking health outcomes were among those the U.S. ended.

Congress had originally allocated about $10 billion to the government’s main global health programs, or roughly $30 per U.S. resident, to run one of the world’s most effective foreign aid efforts. But even after the wave of staff terminations and grant cancellations, Congress still wanted that money to be spent. To direct the funds, last September, the U.S. State Department released a new plan: the America First Global Health Strategy.

This plan endorsed some goals that experts have long championed regardless of political fealty, such as having recipient countries take more responsibility for running and funding the programs.

But it also had a distinctly Trumpian element that seemed shocking to observers of the foreign aid world: The money had significant — and unusual — strings attached. Countries that receive aid were invited to negotiate “America First” agreements with the United States “that promote our national interests while saving millions of lives,” according to a letter from Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

What does this look like in practice? A country that wants aid, for instance, is now asked to share with the United States pathogen samples and access to its health data systems. And in at least several cases, as a health aid agreement was being discussed, the United States was also separately negotiating to gain access to a country’s strategic minerals or to have the country accept U.S. deportees from other nations. State Department representatives have said that these negotiations are not linked, but officials from a number of countries said they had felt pressured to accept terms that were uncomfortable to them.

Many people in countries that receive aid are realists, in that they assume that donors have ulterior motives. Previous efforts to help were never purely selfless. For decades, Democratic and Republican administrations alike have embraced a duality of global public health: framing it in terms of altruism to those in need while also going to lengths to explain to Congress and the American people why promoting a healthier world benefits America.

What, if anything, then, is different about the Trump administration’s insistence that foreign aid dollars deliver a “return for the American people”?

In 2005, I was an aid worker a few years out of medical school when a devastating earthquake struck Pakistan. U.S.A.I.D. was seeking organizations to implement a $28.5 million, four-year health care recovery program. The agency, in its request for applications, said it would select districts based on the extent of earthquake damage, but also on “geopolitical importance to U.S. Government” and “public relations optic.”

More than two decades later, I still remember reading this passage and being struck by its incongruity with the rest of a 46-page technical document focused on improving community health. Aid workers were far from naïve. We knew that donors had their own priorities and that our presence fostered good will toward our home countries too.

Still, it was jarring to read these words from U.S.A.I.D. while spending time with people who had barely survived disaster and were now living under tarps. In the late 20th century, independence had become a core value of humanitarian action. This meant that aid groups responded to people’s needs, not to countries’ political, economic or military objectives.

For governments funding the aid, however, the assistance has long been tied to strategic goals. In an earlier era, aid was often a colonial project. European powers had strong reasons to spend money on health care in lands they had taken over: to keep subjugated workers on the job.

Around the turn of the 20th century, the United States began leading efforts in the Americas to control diseases, including malaria and yellow fever, that were inhibiting trade and travel and frustrating efforts to build the Panama Canal. The U.S. government was a driving force in the creation of the Pan American Health Organization, and later the World Health Organization.

During the Cold War, under Presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson, food aid was positioned as both a way to dispose of surplus U.S. production and to expand markets overseas, in addition to helping “friendly nations.” Congress established U.S.A.I.D. in 1961 to consolidate foreign aid efforts, not least out of an appreciation for aid’s soft power in the fight against Communism.

Not everyone in Washington was convinced, though. Beginning in the 1970s, Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina pushed an isolationist view. He famously referred to foreign aid as pouring money down a “rat hole,” calling it a waste of taxpayers’ resources and a conduit for liberal agendas. Helms tried to abolish U.S.A.I.D. during the Clinton administration. Congress also considered merging the agency into the State Department, in part to give the secretary of state “more direct control over all tools of U.S. foreign policy,” as a Congressional Research Service report put it.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

But in the early 21st century, a bipartisan agreement began to emerge that global health aid was a necessary force for good, in and of itself. This was a direct response to the devastating AIDS epidemic, which has claimed an estimated 44 million lives around the world.

AIDS drugs had become miraculous lifesavers in rich countries but were unavailable in poorer countries. Even Helms, who had blamed homosexuality for the spread of AIDS and opposed funding for research on the disease, was eventually moved. In 2000, he helped write legislation that authorized funds to support AIDS treatment in low-income countries. “I’m so ashamed that I’ve done so little,” he later said at a conference organized by Samaritan’s Purse, a Christian aid organization that participates in the longstanding tradition of missionary and religious-backed global heath assistance.

In 2003, President George W. Bush made the stunning announcement that the United States would commit $15 billion over five years fighting the disease abroad. It was “for a clear reason, directly rooted in our founding,” he said. “We believe in the value and dignity of every human life.” The program became known as the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR.

For years, the C.I.A. had warned that the wave of AIDS deaths could cause global destabilization. However, just two years after the Sept. 11 attacks, humanitarian justifications for PEPFAR featured far more prominently than arguments that it would bolster national security. For years to come, the right and the left supported global health using a rhetoric of compassion and expecting a return on investment in the currency of human lives. PEPFAR still accounts for close to half of the government’s global health aid budget.

An irony of the Trump administration’s more transactional approach to global aid is that it risks losing not only important gains in human health, but also the good will and influence long reaped from U.S. investments. For example, America no longer has a voice in W.H.O. negotiations that could determine how quickly U.S. companies and universities gain access to pathogen information and samples from across the globe in future outbreaks.

In the year since the America First Global Health Strategy was first unveiled, the administration has shared few details on implementation. But the plan is off to a rocky start, according to outside analysts and advocacy groups, among them Public Citizen, which had to sue under the Freedom of Information Act to obtain copies of some of the bilateral deals. Emily Bass, a writer and former State Department consultant, has also revealed details of the initiatives, such as that the U.S. government was asking countries to share specimens of new pathogens that could cause epidemics.

The government’s goal was to sign the bulk of the America First health deals by last December. But it reached agreements with just 14 out of 71 recipient countries. The number has now increased to 36, and at least three countries have explicitly rejected the offers. At a recent meeting with international partners, Brad Smith, a State Department adviser, said the number of deals made represented $14 billion of United States investment, which he called “tremendous progress” in a short time. Those that have been completed have faced difficulties: Kenya’s government was the first country to sign one, only to face two lawsuits challenging the constitutionality of requirements to share data on patients and pathogens with the United States. The courts are allowing implementation to begin while the cases proceed.

Similar provisions were reportedly dropped from an America First health agreement with Zambia, which had objected to them. (U.S. officials say that in all cases, the intention was never for the United States to collect personal health information but rather data on the program’s results.)

Zambian officials also balked after the State Department described aid to the country as being made “in exchange for collaboration in the mining sector,” among other terms. After months of delay, the countries recently signed the health agreement and are still discussing mining deals.

Dr. Atul Gawande was U.S.A.I.D.’s assistant administrator for global health under the Biden administration. He says it is a misnomer to call the America First approach to global health aid “transactional.” He prefers “extractive and predatory.”

“We made transactional deals all the time when I was in the office,” Gawande says. These were expectations around “common goals,” he said, such as reducing child mortality and corruption.

Dr. Mark Dybul, who helped design and later led PEPFAR, says a better way to look at the current U.S. approach to global health is as “a model of mutual benefit.” If countries identify spaces in which they have mutual interests, he says, “then everyone wins.” That could include mining in some cases, because “countries also need extraction of their resources in order for them to grow economically.”

In the end, what will matter most is not the America First Global Health Strategy’s rhetoric, but rather what it aims to accomplish, and whether it will succeed. A major aspect of all of the bilateral agreements available to date involves recipient governments’ agreeing to spend more of their own money on their health systems, a goal shared by African heads of state.

Governments should use more “public resources to finance their people’s health care,” says Tolbert Nyenswah, a former Liberian government health official who now serves as country director for the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in South Sudan.

Only a few years after PEPFAR started as an emergency program, American officials began planning for some countries to take more responsibility for AIDS prevention and treatment. The first Trump administration took steps to promote country self-reliance by increasing the proportion of health programs implemented by local entities, an effort that continued under Biden. The successes showed that “even more radical transition is possible on a fairly short time frame,” says William Steiger, who served as U.S.A.I.D.’s chief of staff during Trump’s first term. Still, for some countries, a rapid shift to self-sufficiency is unlikely. Smith, the State Department adviser, said at the recent meeting that the agreements vary based on national abilities.

“The opportunity for a new approach, a transition to something exciting and different is there,” Dybul says. “It’s going to be based on how we all decide to work with each other again.”

Congress’s actions matter, too. The funding levels in the bilateral health deals obtained to date call for major reductions in aid, according to an analysis by Public Citizen and Partners in Health, and a separate review by the Center for Global Development. For now, however, despite the Trump administration’s proposals for sharp cuts, legislators have appropriated only slightly less money for global health. A Democrat-controlled Congress may be even more willing to fund development aid and scrutinize how the administration is restructuring it.

In recent weeks, the State Department announced a flurry of funding awards for global health. At least one large contract went to a company that had no international development experience, but had ties to the Trump family, and the administration intends to shift many millions of dollars away from reproductive care. Despite reports of the end of American global health aid, the tradition isn’t over. But it is evolving.

item.title: American Roosters Fight in the Philippines Despite U.S. Crackdown
item.description:
Jerry Jalandoni navigated hundreds of chickens running loose on his farm in the Philippines before stopping at a row of tall cages that held his latest acquisitions: a dozen cockfighting roosters from the United States.

On top of one cage was a cardboard box, poked with holes that had allowed a hen to breathe during her solitary journey from Texas to Bacolod City. “She’s been through a lot,” Mr. Jalandoni said.

The hen arrived alone, he said, because her mate had been held back by exporters wary of attracting the attention of animal rights groups. Such birds come from game fowl breeds developed in the United States that are renowned internationally for their sturdiness and aggression — qualities valued in cockfighting, a legal and highly profitable industry in the Philippines.

Those birds were not supposed to be on Mr. Jalandoni’s farm, according to U.S. federal laws. But they are part of a trade in which breeders in the United States send fighting roosters to the Philippines.

While the trade has long been an open secret, the channels through which American fighting birds arrive in Asia are drawing fresh scrutiny from U.S. officials.

Cockfighting — the practice of tying metal blades, or gaffs, to the legs of roosters that fight each other to the death — has been illegal in the United States since 2008, when Louisiana became the last state to outlaw it. Transporting animals across state lines or out of the country for the purpose of fighting was banned in 1976.

Earlier this year, the Justice Department charged three people in Kentucky with offenses related to breeding and shipping roosters overseas for fighting. Airlines have started banning roosters on flights from the United States to the Philippines. And House lawmakers have introduced a bill to strengthen protections for roosters, including prohibiting the U.S. Postal Service from shipping them between states.

“Cockfighting is cruel, inhumane, and illegal,” Inspector General John Walk of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which is pursuing cases against people who possess, train or trade birds for fighting, said in a statement.

But none of those activities violates laws in the Philippines, where a powerful cockfighting industry thrives on legalized gambling, generating hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue each year. The country hosts international rooster derbies such as the World Slasher Cup, where a champion breeder can win six-figure sums.

The Philippines is one of the largest markets for American game fowl. Buyers there imported more than 63,000 adult game fowl from the United States in 2024, Philippine government data show.

That pipeline helped Mr. Jalandoni build up his prized brood.

The lonely hen at his farm arrived in the Philippines on June 17 as part of a shipment sent by Hang Nhan, a Georgia-based livestock broker known to his customers as Daniel Broker.

The chickens had departed Atlanta and arrived in Manila via Doha on Qatar Airways flights, according to a photo of a waybill attached to crates at Manila’s Ninoy Aquino International Airport that was seen by The New York Times.

Video posted on social media the same day by a Filipino game fowl breeder show long wooden crates lined up at the airport’s cargo terminal, where people collected the livestock.

In the video, workers gathered around a crate that had collapsed, killing the chickens inside. “What a waste,” the breeder wrote.

Qatar Airways said in a statement that it “does not knowingly accept” animals shipped for unlawful purposes and that shipments raising concerns receive “enhanced due diligence.”

Four people with knowledge of Mr. Nhan’s operations, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, said that he became a major exporter of U.S. game fowl by charging lower shipping prices than his competitors.

Mr. Nhan did not respond to multiple attempts to reach him for comment.

He has also shipped chickens to the Philippines through Korean Air, which flies from Dallas and Atlanta to Manila via Seoul, according to cargo waybills provided by a person with knowledge of the operations. Korean Air said in April that it would ban roosters on flights from the United States to the Philippines, after a report from a Washington-based animal rights group, Animal Wellness Action, revealed that farms in Oklahoma and Texas had used the airline to transport fighting roosters.

Still, Mr. Nhan sent more than 900 chickens in two shipments on Korean Air in May, according to two waybills that list him as the sender with an address in Griffin, Ga. Asked about the waybills, Korean Air said in a statement that in addition to the ban, it also checks permits and quarantine certificates before accepting live animals.

The same Georgia address appeared on a Turkish Airlines waybill for a shipment of 720 chickens in April, but with a different sender’s name. About 100 birds in that shipment died before reaching Manila because they were left for hours on the hot tarmac in Istanbul, according to an Animal Wellness Action investigation. Turkish Airlines did not respond to a request for comment.

Wayne Pacelle, the advocacy group’s president, said that Mr. Nhan keeps chickens on a 39-acre property in Griffin that matches the address on the waybills, then ships them overseas from the nearby Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

He has advertised his shipment dates on Facebook, encouraging breeders to send their birds to him. His customers in the Philippines often post photos of crates and boxes to thank Mr. Nhan for safely delivering their game fowl.

The chickens are declared as breeding or exhibition fowl on export health certificates, cargo waybills and customs forms. This allows shippers to skirt U.S. federal laws, Mr. Pacelle said.

Mr. Jalandoni said that he imports roosters not for fighting but for breeding, selling the offspring to customers in the Philippines and across Southeast Asia. He enters some in fights, too, according to his social media posts, including a video he shared on Facebook in September showing himself carrying a large rooster into a cockpit.

Game fowl are typically sold as pairs or trios, with at least one hen, he said. A trio from the United States costs importers at least $1,000, plus a shipping fee of up to $200 a bird.

U.S. federal prosecutors have linked at least one American breeder to cockfights in the Philippines. Christopher Copas, who won the 2019 World Slasher Cup in Manila, was among the people indicted on charges in September related to breeding and selling roosters for cockfighting.

Ramon and Eric Escamilla, a father and son in Kentucky, were also indicted in September on charges of shipping roosters to buyers in countries including Mexico and the Philippines, the authorities said.

Neither Mr. Copas nor his lawyer responded to requests for comment. Alan Simpson, a lawyer for the Escamillas, said his clients had pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The cockfighting industry in the Philippines is worth more than $784 million, according to a 2017 estimate by the country’s sports betting regulator that is frequently cited by U.S. officials.

Animal rights activists helped pass the country’s first law against animal cruelty in 1998. Anna Cabrera, the executive director of the Philippine Animal Welfare Society, said pressure at the time from politicians, many of whom are involved in the cockfighting industry, forced the removal of a ban on the practice from the bill.

“They always use culture as an excuse, but the truth is it would interfere with their business,” she said.

The Philippines’ Bureau of Animal Industries and Bureau of Customs did not respond to requests for comment.

Some politicians own cockfighting arenas in the provinces outside Manila.

In Talisay, a town near Bacolod City, the local cockpit is owned by the mayor’s family. During a derby in July, bettors passed bills to the cashier as two roosters engaged in a 10-minute bout, slashing at each other with blades tied to their legs. The winning bird was badly wounded and taken to a farmhand, who gave it stitches in a blood-spattered area away from the fighting. Dozens of other farmhands rushed around, passing chickens to be stitched up or prepared for fights.

What if the rooster doesn’t recover?

“Adobo,” said Mark Kelley, an American breeder in Bacolod City, naming a popular Filipino chicken dish.

Mr. Jalandoni, who was still waiting for his missing rooster and about 20 other chickens that he had ordered from Texas, said he doubted that a ban would be able to reverse centuries of cockfighting culture.

Besides, he said, the pipeline was open long enough for Filipino breeders to establish American game fowl bloodlines locally.

Despite the scrutiny from activists and U.S. authorities, the demand for American game fowl remains strong. In mid-October, Mr. Nhan sent his first shipment of the fall to the Philippines. It contained 800 birds, according to a Qatar Airways cargo waybill. The airline did not respond to a request for comment on the shipment.

On Facebook, Mr. Nhan’s associates still post videos and photos of game fowl shipping crates — and receive dozens of comments inquiring about their services.

item.title: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
item.description:
There was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.

We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.

My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.

By David Gelles

It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Now, just 11 years after the target was set, it’s effectively dead.

Scientists now say that without increasingly drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases — more drastic than the ones humans have tried and failed at so far — it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6ºC by the end of the century.

At COP31, the ongoing United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target have been blunt.

“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

Tipping points

Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5ºC, compared with preindustrial levels, would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.

That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a summer of European heat waves killed an estimated 50,000 people.

Should warming continue unabated, scientists say the world may cross certain tipping points, including the melting of Arctic permafrost, the rapid decline of rainforests and a slowdown of a key current in the Atlantic Ocean.

The 1.5 degrees target was always ambitious. Achieving it would have required wealthy countries to make the biggest changes, with potentially profound effects on their economies. Cost, politics and inertia all got in the way.

As a result, one big question at the climate talks has been whether the world should set a new goal. But most people I spoke with said no.

“We don’t think that there’s a new target,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the United Nations. “We still have a Paris Agreement target of 1.5, and so we are still continuing to say that’s the target.”

Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, warned against picking a new target, saying that it was important to confront what breaching the threshold has wrought.

“I don’t think it’s a question of replacing 1.5,” she said. “There is no new number. We are now in the unsafe zone.”

Leaders rejected the idea of resetting the goal to 2ºC or even 2.5ºC, saying that allowing for endless revisions created a slippery slope that could make progress harder to achieve.

A temporary breach?

While world leaders acknowledged they had missed the target, they also said it might still be possible to get back to 1.5 degrees of warming.

The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, called on countries to redouble efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions with the aim of limiting additional warming, and ultimately turning down Earth’s thermostat.

“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be,” he said. “We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence.”

So far, the world has crossed the 1.5 threshold for only a few months. But emissions continue at near-record levels. Although clean energy is growing rapidly, the world is expected to continue to use fossil fuels for decades to come.

At this point, meeting the emissions targets set in Paris wouldn’t be enough to bring the temperature rise back down from 1.5 degrees. It would require drastic reductions in the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas — and possibly more.

Because reducing emissions is proving so difficult, some environmentalists and scientists are proposing different types of geoengineering. These include large-scale carbon capture and storage or attempts to reflect the sun’s energy away from the planet by injecting particulate matter into the stratosphere.

“Overshoot must be kept as small and short as possible, and be rapidly reversed,” said Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, an island nation threatened by sea-level rise. “We have fallen short of the emissions reductions needed to stay under 1.5. We must rewrite the future.”

Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has started bombing the Ukrainian infrastructure that provides heat and running water in the winter, threatening to make some cities unlivable.

Tripp Mickle, one of our technology reporters, examines in the video below how Huang had immense power within Nvidia and the broader A.I. sector.

Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges, accusing them of colluding with Iran.

Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over. Robert Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007, one of the most coveted and unforgiving roles in moviedom. He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he was ending his celebrated five-film run.

Ron Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago. Israel’s long search for him has come to symbolize the country’s commitment to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive.

Several Israeli intelligence reports have concluded that Iran was not involved in Arad’s disappearance. Yet time and again, a New York Times investigation found, Israeli officials gave credence to reports that Iran was to blame for the disappearance, or knew Arad’s whereabouts. The singer Vivir Quintana flips that formula, although her subject matter is still violent: One corrido was based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes. She made one album that included 10 corridos about women who fought back against their attackers only to end up behind bars.

“I used to think that what united us women was our pain,” Quintana told a crowd at a recent event. “Now, I have realized it is love and resistance.” Read more about her career.

item.title: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
item.description:
The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.

Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.

Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.

“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”

Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

Before the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China, this week, Mr. Carney will have his second formal meeting this year with China’s leader, Xi Jinping. And Mr. Carney, who is as fond of free trade agreements as Mr. Trump is of tariffs, announced in Manila before the ASEAN meetings opened that Canada had completed the broad negotiations for a deal with the Philippines. Talks are also underway on a wider trade arrangement with all 11 ASEAN countries.

On Saturday, Mr. Carney said that at both summits he would press his call for “middle powers” to unite and would present Canada as a reliable alternative to an increasingly unpredictable United States as a supplier of important products like oil and gas.

“It’s part of our strategy, absolutely, 100 percent,” Mr. Carney said at a news conference after meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. “We’re very transparent about it. It’s a part of our strategy to develop this dense web of connections to make us resilient, to make us more independent, to make us sovereign so we can live our lives as we choose, so we’re not being told what to do by some hegemon or a hyperscaler.”

“It is to varying degrees part of the strategies of many, many countries,” he added, “and that’s one of the reasons why you’re seeing so much progress.”

Between the Asia summits, Mr. Carney made a quick stop in Cambodia, which is hosting a meeting of the International Organization of Francophonie, an association that promotes French language and culture. There, he received noticeably more applause than anyone else when the leaders were introduced.

During the APEC meeting, however, Mr. Carney will come up hard against superpower politics. Mr. Xi will host a meeting with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and Mr. Trump. Mr. Putin’s appearance, after he skipped last year’s APEC meeting in South Korea, is a stark contrast with the European Political Community summit in Dublin. There, Mr. Carney and his European counterparts reaffirmed their unqualified support for Ukraine at a meeting also attended by its leader, President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Mr. Carney said he would pose for a group photograph of the APEC leaders with Mr. Putin “out of respect for the host.”

But that appears to be Mr. Carney’s limit. He again noted on Saturday that Canada would bar Russian and Belarusian teams from entering the country for the Men’s World Junior Hockey Championship at the end of the year.

“Canada stands firmly with Ukraine, firmly with democracy, territorial integrity, rule of law,” he said. “All of those put us on the other side of Vladimir Putin’s Russia.”

Canada’s relationship with China, the biggest potential market for replacing trade with the United States, was sulfurous before Mr. Carney, a former governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, entered politics last year.

It collapsed after China arrested two Canadians in what was widely seen in Canada as hostage-taking in retaliation for Canada’s arrest of a Chinese telecommunications executive on a U.S. extradition request. An inquiry also concluded that China had tried to interfere in Canadian politics.

Polls suggest that Canadians’ good will toward China has risen since Mr. Carney re-established relations. At the same time, their views of the United States under Mr. Trump, who started a trade war and continues to suggest that Canada should be the 51st American state, have moved decidedly in the other direction.

But Mr. Carney will be limited in how far he can go with China. A poll by the nonprofit Angus Reid Institute found that only 14 percent of Canadians favor closer trade ties with China. By contrast, 58 percent of respondents want to increase trade ties with Europe.

In January, after meeting with Mr. Xi, Mr. Carney predicted that Chinese automakers would make substantial investments in Canada within three years.

On Saturday, however, he was more circumspect. While the government wants “a competitive Canadian auto sector that produces good-paying jobs, good union jobs for Canadian workers,” he said, it also wants Canadians to have access to affordable electric cars.

“There are multiple variables, and there’s multiple ways to achieve those objectives,” he said. “It depends partially on — and importantly on — where the U.S. trading relationship settles out.”

item.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
item.description:
To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife.

Then she sets up a trap along that path.

“We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland.

“We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.”

Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke, a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled.

The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year.

Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer.

Tourists are drawn to its golden beaches, crystalline water and wineries. But for stoats, it’s all about the birds.

Stoats, known also as short-tailed weasels in North America, have reddish-brown fur and a white underbelly, and can measure about 39 centimeters, or 15 inches, from nose to tip of tail. They were initially introduced to New Zealand from Britain in the late 1870s to control the population of rabbits, which themselves were introduced for food and sport in the country as early as the 1830s.

The carnivores quickly turned their appetites to New Zealand’s native birds, many of which evolved to be flightless because the islands were isolated for millions of years and had no ground-dwelling predators.

Stoats, like other animals introduced by Europeans to New Zealand such as goats, rats and red deer, have pushed several species to the brink of extinction, either as predators or through habitat destruction.

If Te Korowai o Waiheke successfully eradicates them, it will create the world’s first predator-free urban island, possibly forming a blueprint for others to follow. New Zealand has bold plans to be free of predator-free by 2050, and other programs are underway to eradicate other invasive species.

Mary Morgan-Richards, evolutionary biology professor at Massey University Manawatū, said keeping people and governments committed to the goal — and ensuring ample funding — will be crucial.

Te Korowai o Waiheke — a name bestowed by the local iwi (tribe), the Ngāti Paoa — is funded by the country’s environment department as well as the local council and philanthropic organizations.

Growing up on the island, Ms. Sorensen, 30, said she rarely saw native birds like the kākā, a type of parrot, or the pāteke, a dabbling duck, which the team refers to as “stoat chocolates.”

But in the past six years, these birds have returned in large numbers, Ms. Sorensen said.

Each year, experienced bird spotters record everything they hear and see across 70 sites on the island over five minutes. Figures from November 2020 versus 2025 show a 99.6 percent increase in native birds counted, including a 930 percent increase in kākā birds, of which there are estimated to be fewer than 10,000 left.

And 24 flightless kiwi birds, the country’s unofficial national emblem, have been reintroduced to the island in the past couple of years and successfully bred, an effort led by another conservation group and local tribes. Those on the island say it has been a long time since kiwi birds freely wandered the shores.

While walking in the forest, Ms. Sorensen regularly pauses conversations to point out the calls of the kākā as it flies nearby.

“Sometimes you’ve just got to stop and listen and go, ‘oh my god’,” she said.

“Conservation in general in New Zealand is a little bit strange in that most of it is killing stuff,” she said.

The team uses a range of measures to catch the stoats, including motion cameras and 1,600 traps laced with lures that might entice them. These could include stoat anal scent glands, soiled stoat bedding, fried chicken or duck fat.

The team also installs small fences along stoat pathways that direct the pest into traps by blocking escape routes. A further 200 traps are installed by the team across the island following sightings by members of the public or using dogs that are trained to sniff out stoat feces.

The response team and volunteers are constantly brainstorming for new ideas that might help capture the remaining animals. They work across the island, sometimes hiking for miles into the bush to set or check traps, sometimes finding nothing.

To keep the team motivated, Frank Lepera, stoat operations manager, tells them: “You never know when a stoat is having a bad day.”

“You have to have every single trap in like perfect condition, so when it is having a bad day and it walks by that trap, it goes in.”

On the day The New York Times visited, the team responded to a stoat sighting reported by a person who had seen it dashing across the front lawn, into the scrub and beach below.

The team placed traps along different routes, each one laced with a combination of lures including canned sardines, rabbit blood or a recording of stoat babies (known as kits). They work like a giant mousetrap to kill the stoat, and were to be checked every few days.

Once caught, the dead stoat’s tail and ears are sent off for genetic testing — the island’s population is inbred, so testing can show if there have been any new incursions from other islands. The stoat’s teeth are used to determine its age — a decline in younger ones would mean the stoats may be breeding less as the adult population shrinks.

While there is no way of knowing exactly how many furry predators remain, the increasingly empty traps and return of native birds indicate that the stoat population is declining.

There are a few notorious stoats that have managed to evade the team. One of them is called the “Lion’s Tail” — named after a bald spot on its tail that resembles a lion’s. It is often seen darting in front of the motion cameras but has not ended up in a trap, yet.

Ms. Sorensen joked that she will bake a stoat-shaped cake on the day it is finally vanquished.

Many in the team said they dream of chasing or catching stoats.

Phil Salisbury, a team leader, said the days are long and the work is hard, but the reward is “flying around us.”

“Every bird you hear, especially the kākā and stuff, it’s a success story,” he said.

item.title: They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?
item.description:
They had no leader, no political party and no conventional campaign. They made decisions by raising their hands after hours of debate in university classrooms, a slow and cumbersome process billed as a unique experiment in direct democracy.

That free-form approach to politics of Serbia’s students proved so effective that, in a general election on Oct. 25, they achieved what established opposition parties had failed to accomplish for more than a decade: routing the well-oiled political machine of Serbia’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic.

Mr. Vucic, nearing the end of his second term as president and barred from running again, had resigned as president a month before the October vote for a new Parliament, gambling that his governing party would win and that he could keep his grip on power by becoming prime minister. He had held that post twice before.

His plan was upended by the election victory of a slate of parliamentary candidates selected by students in freewheeling campus meetings. Their selections and electoral successes marked the culmination of a striking exercise in collective decision making. That approach, some believe, could hold lessons for democratic movements beyond Serbia.

But the principles that carried the students to victory may not, on their own, be enough to build a functioning, coherent and durable government.

The diverse list of candidates chosen by the students, nearly all political novices with a wide range of sometimes contradictory views, reflected a belief that everyone should have a say in a leaderless movement united by the single objective of getting rid of Mr. Vucic and the system he created.

Yet the group decision-making process, which the students called “plenums,” was often opaque and presented a fundamental problem, said Vladimir Vuletic, a sociologist.

“It is a combination of Communist-style decision making through plenums and democratic decision making through elected members of Parliament,” he said. “Reconciling these two approaches will be an organizational challenge.”

“Ideological and organizational differences will inevitably lead to divisions within the movement and probably to new elections within a year,” he added.

Students acknowledge that Serbia’s yet-to-be-formed new government cannot be run along the same lines as the student assemblies.

“The future Parliament and government will not operate according to the principles of student plenums and direct democracy, but according to constitutional principles and the program we developed together with our candidates and other experts,” said Natalija Petrovic, 22, a communications and public relations student.

Before the election, the student plenums spent hours debating even minor proposals. The government may not have that luxury and will need to approve budgets, appoint ministers, negotiate international agreements and respond to crises in a timely way.

Even stickier perhaps is that the students, who chose not to put themselves forward as candidates, still hope to maintain oversight over the people they selected for the winning slate, called Student List-Students Win.

They insist they have no plans to reproduce their plenum assemblies inside government ministries, but they want to supervise legislators as an independent force outside Parliament, demanding transparency and accountability.

There has been no word yet on who will become prime minister to lead the new government, which will take shape once the newly elected Parliament convenes. No date has been set for that, but it must happen within three months of the release of the final official results on Nov. 5.

Those results gave the Student List a hefty majority with 140 seats in Serbia’s 250-member legislature, compared with just 103 for Mr. Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party.

Student List candidates have committed to a 1,000-page governing program developed with the involvement of thousands of experts, professors and students. The program is long on commitments to abstract principles like accountability, and short on concrete plans. It largely avoids divisive issues, particularly in foreign policy.

Students, though, have made clear their desire to end Mr. Vucic’s close cooperation with Israel on defense and other matters. Their program promised not “to be complicit in the systematic attempt to destroy the Palestinian people by Israel in the Gaza Strip.”

The student movement began in November 2024 after the collapse of a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station in Serbia’s second biggest city, Novi Sad. The disaster killed 16 people and became a symbol of what students, who immediately took to the streets, see as Serbia’s systemic corruption under Mr. Vucic.

Nikola Maletic, 21, a political science student, was only yards away when the canopy fell.

The protest movement’s lack of a leader, he said, was initially a tactic to stay off the radar of security forces but later became a matter of principle.

“People realized that we must never again allow one man to run the country,” he said.

Demanding the arrest and trial of construction contractors and officials accused of approving shoddy work, the students occupied university buildings and staged street protests, some of which drew hundreds of thousands of people, for nearly two years. They began holding plenums to decide how to push forward demands for accountability.

The movement struck a chord with many people outside university campuses, who were also fed up with corruption. It reached beyond big cities like Belgrade, the capital, long hostile to Mr. Vucic, to penetrate places that had long supported his governing party.

The students walked and cycled hundreds of miles across Serbia, visiting small towns and remote villages where opposition politicians had rarely won support. They sat with farmers, spoke with parents and pensioners, and listened to people who had lost faith in politics.

Such encounters helped build a national movement.

While Mr. Vucic dominated reports by the national broadcasters, the students relied on social media and an unconventional decision-making system.

Radomir Saicic, a chemistry professor and candidate on the Student List, described the plenums as a form of “horizontal democracy.”

The process was slow and demanding, but was also meant to be deliberately diffuse.

“The idea behind a leaderless movement was that an authoritarian regime could not target and discredit a single individual and, in doing so, undermine the entire movement,” recalled Ms. Petrovic, the communications student.

The plenums to select candidates for the election were held in secret, with phones left outside and would-be contenders assigned changing code names to prevent leaks.

Students nominated and questioned the candidates, checked their backgrounds and put them up to a vote. The candidates were then reviewed by university departments across Serbia, with support of more than half of them needed to make the final list.

Each candidate was asked to sign “social contracts” committing to the movement’s principles and objectives.

The result is that even though the Student List was made up of people with different views, they all agreed on the government’s central purpose, Ms. Petrovic said.

“Our government’s main goal is to wrest the state from the grip of the mafia and create mechanisms of accountability and transparency that will make corruption as difficult as possible for any future government,” she said.

How the relationship between students and the winning candidates they selected will now evolve is still unclear. Difficult questions remain about what will happen when elected representatives disagree with the movement that brought them to power.

“The ruling phase would require that M.P.s or ministries gain real authority, freed from students’ control,” Dusan Spasojevic, a political science professor at the University of Belgrade, wrote in a study of the movement.

But students are wary of giving legislators a free hand, fearing this could create a new power center beyond their control, much like Serbia’s established political parties.

“The only real victory will be a lasting change in the political culture and the way the country is governed,” said Mr. Maletic, the student who narrowly avoided being crushed at the railway station in Novi Sad. “Anything else would simply mean a new government behaving like the old one.”

Andrew Higgins contributed reporting.
