item.title: South Korea to Examine How K-Pop Industry Treats Underage Performers
item.description:
South Korea’s government is planning to study how the K-pop industry treats underage performers, who are central to the industry, and to re-examine the standard template for contracts it released nearly two decades ago.

The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism will start an industrywide survey sometime next year, a ministry official said in a telephone interview on Monday. The government already studies the K-pop industry, checking whether record companies follow its standard contract and how much money is invested in training young stars. The new effort will focus specifically on how underage artists are treated, but its methodology, scope and exact timeline have not been decided on.

The announcement came just over a week after The New York Times published an investigation into the record contracts signed by the members of NewJeans, one of K-pop’s biggest girl groups, when they were ages 14 to 17. The investigation found that the contracts removed language included in the government template that guarantees rights for minors, such as the rights to education and sleep.

It was a rare look into the business of K-pop, which has long been dogged by allegations of exploitation. Record companies recruit children who are aspiring stars, put them through years of intensive training and then often bill them for those costs. Several stars have died by suicide.

Two years ago, NewJeans tried to quit their label in a dispute that turned into one of K-pop’s most public fights, with the members saying they had been mistreated. A court later held them to the contracts they had signed, which run until 2029.

The Seoul Broadcasting System reported the ministry’s plan earlier.

In 2009, after a boy band sued its label over restrictive work agreements, the authorities created a standard contract. It outlined protections such as capping agreements at seven years, taking into consideration an artist’s physical and mental well-being and transferring trademark rights to the artist after the terms end.

The template has been amended several times over the years but still largely remains legally nonbinding. Record companies often alter clauses and add their own conditions. Some do not use the template at all, a government survey found.

item.title: Trump’s Asia Trip Will Bring Him to the Table With Xi and Putin
item.description:
President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.

For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.

The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.

The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.

The White House has said that Mr. Trump wants to discuss the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about China’s accelerating nuclear buildup, expected to reach 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030.

The last nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February. Trump administration officials have said that any new agreement on nuclear arms control must include China, but Beijing has shown no interest in the topic. China has an estimated 620 nuclear warheads, compared with the more than 5,000 that Russia and the United States have each, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

U.S. administration officials said they did not expect a deal out of the meeting, which they characterized as a starting point for discussions.

The gathering has prompted concern in Ukraine that Mr. Putin might push for a deal, deciding Ukraine’s fate without Kyiv’s involvement. A U.S. administration official said Ukraine was not expected to be part of the discussion between the three leaders.

Mr. Trump will start his trip in the Philippines, the oldest American treaty ally in the Asia-Pacific region, as the United States faces questions about its support for its partners in a region where China’s military and economic might continues to grow.

In Manila, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. plans to discuss with Mr. Trump the South China Sea, where the Philippines and China have competing claims. Philippine officials have said that they hope Mr. Trump’s visit might result in more American military assistance.

Mr. Trump is also expected to meet with leaders of ASEAN, a Southeast Asian grouping of 11 nations, as well as a gathering of the so-called Quad grouping of the United States, India, Australia and Japan.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia said on Sunday that he expected “lots of engagement” with Mr. Trump during the meetings.

“Obviously, that’s our most important ally,” he said. “But we want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts that are around the world.”

Chinese analysts described the meeting of the Quad group, formed in part to counter China, as an effort by Mr. Trump to project power after his party’s defeat in the midterms. “Its symbolic value outweighs its practical value,” Xu Liping, a senior scholar at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, told Shanghai Observer, a state-run outlet.

After Manila, Mr. Trump will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, where he will meet Mr. Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

Jensen Huang, a key adviser who accompanied Mr. Trump on his last trip to China, will not be by his side. Mr. Huang helped shape the president’s views about technological competition with China and persuaded him to loosen restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.

Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was collecting intelligence on Mr. Huang for Beijing. China has rejected the allegations, calling them “smears.” Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

So far, the president has not raised the issue with Mr. Xi and is not expected to during their meeting on Thursday. But the saga is likely to cause unease in China about whether Washington will impose tighter controls on the export of technology to the country.

As a result, U.S.-based analysts speculated that Mr. Xi might try to use his personal relationship with Mr. Trump to forestall such restrictions.

Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, said Mr. Huang’s downfall would likely mean “there is going to be more anxiety on the Chinese side about their access to American chips.” She expects Mr. Xi to emphasize the importance of easing U.S. controls on chip exports to China during their meeting.

Cooperation between China and the United States on artificial intelligence may be more difficult after the Nvidia scandal.

Still, there may be progress on the creation of a notification system that would allow the countries to alert each other about national security issues related to artificial intelligence, which the two sides agreed to in September.

“There’s some shared concern on both sides that U.S. or Chinese models might be misused by bad actors and cause damage to the U.S., China, or other countries,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution focusing on China’s technology development.

When Mr. Xi sits down with Mr. Trump in Shenzhen, he will be dealing with a president who will soon face a new constraint at home: a Democrat-controlled Congress.

Lawmakers may pressure Mr. Trump to tighten export controls against China or accelerate weapons sales to Taiwan, according to Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser focusing on U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group. That means that “Xi will have to work much harder to keep Trump on side,” Mr. Wyne said.

Mr. Trump will be the first American president to visit China twice in one calendar year.

Analysts say the leaders’ summits, which have included state visits in Beijing and then in Washington, have been the only thing holding together a fragile détente between the two countries as they clash over A.I., export controls, Taiwan and other issues.

The two sides declared a trade truce last year when they met in Busan, South Korea. That deal, which was to expire this month, has been extended until January.

China’s restrictions on the export of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets, which are needed to manufacture most modern technology, remain one of the most difficult unresolved issues.

Mr. Trump is likely to raise this with Mr. Xi, according to a senior U.S. administration official who said that China’s continued restrictions is one reason Washington only agreed to a two-month extension of the trade truce.

item.title: Relentless Attacks on Ukraine’s Power Grid Threaten to Make Cities Unlivable
item.description:
When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi, the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations.

But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said. Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months.

In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring.

“They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack.

The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine.

Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses.

United Nations investigators have condemned Russia’s pummeling of dense urban centers with ballistic missiles and glide bombs as crimes against humanity. The latest Russian campaign is engineering a punishing new reality for Ukrainians: rolling blackouts and water shut-offs as weakened transmission systems leave power stranded at generation plants, unable to reach cities.

Kyiv is the main target. Viktoriia Bulakh, 43, said her apartment building on the outskirts of the city had recently been receiving just 18 to 26 minutes of power a day.

Without electricity, her building has no heating, no running water and no working elevators. During nighttime air-raid alerts, she and her 9-year-old son trudge down nine flights of stairs to a freezing basement shelter and then back up again when an all-clear is given.

“All night, back and forth,” she said. “Up the stairs, down the stairs. Up, down, up again.”

They recently slept through nearby explosions, and Ms. Bulakh said she had noticed that her neighbor had stopped going to the basement with her toddler because it was just too hard. “The little ones are sleepy,” she said. “They want to sleep. They cry, poor little things.”

Ukrainian officials and aid groups warn of a looming humanitarian crisis if major cities are stripped of heat, running water and sanitation. Among residents with the means to leave for the winter, many are considering doing so.

“Winter is not yet here, and we already don’t have power,” said Maksym Timchenko, the chief executive of DTEK, the country’s largest private energy company and the capital’s electricity distributor.

Winter after grueling winter, Moscow has sought to undermine the Ukrainian will to fight by bombarding critical infrastructure and making life miserable. Year after year, including during the exceptionally cold winter of 2025, Ukraine has found a way to push through.

It is impossible to forecast how Ukraine’s cities will fare this year, and the weather will play a role. Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Energy Industry Research Center in Kyiv, said that the capital could survive the winter without a catastrophic blackout if crews got safe windows between Russian strikes to repair damaged lines.

“No one in the world knows how to operate under attack like we know,” Mr. Kharchenko said. “We are having a very hard time, but we will recover.”

Ukraine’s prospects depend in large part on people like Serhii Tytarenko, who heads a power-line maintenance crew in Sumy, a city in northeastern Ukraine that comes under regular Russian attack. He described being hunted by drones day and night while working in heavy protective gear.

A few days ago, he said, colleagues on their way to make repairs were driving down a busy street in the city when a drone hit their vehicle. One crew member lost a limb, he said.

“Everyone has their own front,” he said. “We are holding our energy front, as we say.”

On Sept. 1, Mr. Putin of Russia ordered a campaign of mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector. By the end of October, Russian forces had launched more than 350 attacks on grid infrastructure, damaging over 800 pieces of critical equipment, according to Ukrainian officials.

Seventy-two hours before the talks began in Abu Dhabi, Moscow launched a salvo of 36 ballistic missiles — very few of which were shot down — and 172 drones. All of the missiles were aimed at Kyiv and its surrounding region. The assault severed high-voltage transmission lines feeding the capital, leaving 40 percent of Kyiv’s residential high-rises without heat before winter’s first hard frost.

More Russian weapons are getting through as Ukraine’s air defense umbrella, once a marvel of patchwork innovation, has begun to fracture in part under the sheer arithmetic of attrition.

Stockpiles of American-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which remain Ukraine’s only reliable shield against ballistic missiles, are running perilously low as Washington conserves supplies for crises in the Middle East and as European allies struggle to procure more missiles.

In an interview, the Ukrainian Air Force spokesman, Col. Yurii Ihnat, said that air-defense crews had abandoned standard doctrine, which calls for firing at least two interceptors at each incoming ballistic missile.

“We cannot afford such a luxury,” Colonel Ihnat said. “We are forced to use one missile on one target — but as you can see, 40 missiles are flying and five of them are being shot down. We just don’t have them anymore.”

Fighter jets remain Ukraine’s primary defense against Russia’s high-altitude jet-powered attack drones. While interception rates for jet-drones can reach 85 to 90 percent during concentrated raids, Colonel Ihnat said that bad weather and dispersed swarms coming from multiple directions could at times lower that rate to 50 or 60 percent.

Compounding the strain, Mr. Zelensky has warned that Ukrainian forces are again experiencing speed restrictions on Starshield, the American satellite network that serves as the military’s communications backbone. That, he said, was hampering Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from jet-powered drones.

Kyiv is waging its own drone campaign inside Russia, targeting major oil refineries and export terminals to choke off the energy revenues funding Moscow’s war machine. The Russian campaign against Ukraine, however, is far broader and more lethal.

In Ukrainian cities, the effects are seen in darkened stairwells and freezing apartments.

Anna Dzebliuk, 25, said that unpredictable electricity outages and water disruptions had derailed her daily routines. She hoards battery power for emergencies, warms her bed with a hot-water bottle during 10-minute power windows, and tailors her eating schedule to when the lights are on — even if it’s midnight and she isn’t hungry.

“It’s strange, because home stops being a safe place for you,” she said. “In the evening, when I come home from work or wherever I’ve been, it feels like I’m coming back to some basement.”

Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting.

item.title: U.N. Starts Uncertain Effort to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons
item.description:
Global efforts to limit the use of lethal autonomous weapons reached a crossroads this week as countries gathered to decide whether to negotiate binding restrictions on the technology, despite strong resistance from the United States and Russia.

Delegates of 128 states met at the United Nations in Geneva on Monday for a weeklong conference to determine whether to draft a treaty that would ban lethal autonomous weapons and require meaningful human control of such systems.

“The longer the international community waits, the more difficult it will become to establish meaningful safeguards — and it may be too late,” Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, said before the conference.

Artificial intelligence and its military uses are developing at breakneck speed, as seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East. That has deepened international alarm and prompted calls for action by many countries, global leaders and activist groups, even as top military powers balk at attempts to curb their ability to develop new weapons.

“Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo XIV said in a statement last month that urged those at the Geneva conference to take “concrete “steps” to ban lethal autonomous weapons. Artificial intelligence, he said, “must be ‘disarmed.’”

Russia and Ukraine have already deployed fully autonomous drones to carry out attacks. Disarmament experts fear that the low cost and easy availability of such technology could lead to its rapid spread to law enforcement, nonstate armed groups and organized crime.

Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, said last week that states had to “ensure that the future of warfare is not handed over to machines.”

It is unclear, however, how much progress will be made in Geneva.

Much of the groundwork needed for a new convention was covered in three years of discussions by governmental experts that ended in September. Those talks aligned states on a working definition of lethal autonomous weapons and on the need to comply with international humanitarian law.

In a move that angered many countries, the United States and Russia intervened in the closing hours of those talks to remove elements that many considered essential. That included language on the need for autonomous weapons to be reliable, predictable and traceable to whoever develops or uses them, and on the need for “a responsible chain of human command and control.”

The final document was still accepted by states and humanitarian organizations as a reasonable basis for negotiating a binding agreement — a process that most countries support. A resolution to that effect was backed by 163 states in the U.N. General Assembly in October, facing opposition from the United States, Israel, Russia, Belarus and North Korea. Nine countries abstained, including China, Iran and Saudi Arabia.

But the format of this week’s discussions in Geneva — which are proceeding under the U.N. Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons — could make it harder to successfully negotiate a binding treaty. The convention’s rule of decision-making by consensus gives every state an effective power of veto on further talks.

States could sidestep that by pursuing negotiations in the U.N. General Assembly or through an independent process, as they did for earlier treaties banning land mines and cluster munitions. But key military powers like the United States would probably pull out of any such process — meaning they would not be bound by any resulting agreement.

There was disagreement about how to proceed before the conference in Geneva had even started.

The Peruvian chair of the discussions on autonomous weapons has proposed giving countries a mandate to negotiate a new protocol within two years. The United States has instead proposed discussing a nonbinding instrument over five years. Autonomy in weapons can enhance compliance with international law, the United States said in a working paper, arguing that it would be contrary to the humanitarian objectives of the convention to “hamper responsible innovation.”

There were also signs of stalling from Russia, which has challenged the way observers can participate in the Geneva talks, leaving it unclear how they will proceed.

Maria Zakharova, a spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, told reporters last week that it wanted to resolve “all organizational matters” before the conference began. In any case, she added: “We consider it premature to argue that the time has supposedly come to develop restrictive or prohibitive measures concerning such systems.”

Proponents of new rules say the talks need to produce a firm commitment to quickly drafting a protocol. Otherwise, they argue, military efforts to develop lethal autonomous weapons will outpace efforts to ban them.

“This is genuinely a do-or-die moment,” said Beatrice Fihn, a disarmament activist who received the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons. “If we don’t start negotiating, and quickly, then we are accepting autonomous weapons will kill people on the battlefields in the next few years.”

item.title: Bahrain Convicts Dozens of Shiite Clerics in Sweeping Terrorism Trial
item.description:
Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government.

The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the trial, saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions.

A lawyer for several of the defendants said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He spoke on the condition of anonymity, fearing retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, and he described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients.

In a statement published by Bahrain’s state news agency, the public prosecution department said that the defendants had been afforded all of their legal rights and given “a fair and equitable trial.”

The statement said that the defendants had formed a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. The department accused the defendants of working to undermine the Bahraini government and said that the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials.

“They had also sought to change the system of government by force and unlawful means through incitement to commit terrorist acts, acts of rioting and sabotage,” the statement added.

Sunnism and Shiism are the two main branches of Islam. While most people in Bahrain are Shiites, the country is ruled by a Sunni royal family, and Shiite citizens have long complained of marginalization and persecution.

The war on Iran has widened those fault lines. As Tehran has fired thousands of missiles and drones at Gulf Arab countries, including Bahrain, that host American military bases, several of those nations have accused Shiite citizens of disloyalty or of conspiring with Iran.

Nearly all of the 69 defendants in the Bahrain case are Shiite clerics, including prominent scholars and imams, according to a joint statement this month from rights groups including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International.

“Since Bahrain’s judiciary was established in the 1920s, the country has never witnessed persecution of Shia clerics on this scale,” said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy, whose organization also signed the statement. “This is an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain’s Shia community.”

Five of the defendants were sentenced to 15 years in prison, while the rest received life sentences, Mr. Alwadaei said.

The statement from the Bahraini public prosecution department did not identify how many people had been convicted, but it said that their sentences ranged from 15 years in prison to life. The Bahraini government did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

More than a decade ago, during the Arab Spring, Bahrain, a U.S. ally, violently crushed a pro-democracy uprising.

The uprising was led by both Shiite and Sunni Bahrainis. In the years since, the authorities have dissolved the main political opposition group, jailed opposition leaders and cracked down on dissent.

Rights groups say the repression has intensified since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. The Bahraini authorities have arrested dozens of citizens on charges including “glorifying or sympathizing with the hostile Iranian acts, or engaging in contacts with external parties.”

In May, the government also stripped scores of Shiite citizens, including many children, of their Bahraini nationality — accusing them of disloyalty, rendering them stateless and attempting to deport them to Iran.

The verdict on Monday convicted the 69 defendants of seeking to promote wilayat al-faqih, the ideology that underpins Iran’s theocratic system. That ideology grants the Iranian supreme leader transnational political and religious authority over Twelver Shiites, a branch of Islam that is Iran’s state religion. Most Bahraini Shiites belong to that branch.

The rights groups said in their joint statement before the verdict that the authorities had cited theological books and instruction, charitable funds and overseas religious contacts as evidence, risking the criminalization of peaceful expressions of faith. They said that some defendants had been held incommunicado and threatened with physical and sexual violence.

Defense lawyers were also denied copies of the evidence, the groups said, while some defendants reported being pressured to sign statements they were not permitted to read. The Bahraini government did not respond to questions about those claims.

In January, the United Nations Committee Against Torture raised concerns over reports that torture was routinely used to extract confessions in Bahrain and that terrorism proceedings lacked procedural safeguards.

item.title: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
item.description:
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.

The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.

The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers.

With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance, making it harder for migrants to reach Europe, and easier for Europe to deport them.

“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday, arguing that the group was pushing for a more “sustainable” and “orderly” asylum and migration system.

“I think this will be a game-changer,” she added.

The pilot project — which is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees — is likely to be fleshed out with more detail in early 2027. Officials have suggested that it could start to send people to Africa later next year.

Critics are worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.

The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.

Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

This is not Europe’s first experiment in funneling migrants toward third countries. Italy tried to set up an asylum processing hub in Albania, though that plan has run into legal challenges.

The five countries involved in this plan argue that it is different from previous efforts. For one thing, it will focus on migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues for staying in Europe, rather than on migrants who are just starting asylum claims. The European Union recently set out a legal framework for third-country return hubs, and this one will be operated along those lines.

But the decision has raised eyebrows.

For some, the choice of Rwanda is concerning. The nation often ranks low on human rights measures, especially when it comes to free speech. It has also faced sanctions from the United States and criticism from Europe, which have accused it of supporting a rebel militia in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“Its human rights record is very, very dodgy,” said Toni Haastrup, professor and chair in global politics at the University of Manchester.

Mélissa Camara, a member of European Parliament, objects to return hubs as a concept, saying they did not do enough to guarantee human rights. On Monday, she called the Rwanda plan “an agreement of shame, a grave moral failing.”

The nations leading the charge insist that human rights will be protected. And they say that deporting people to Rwanda could bring big benefits, including discouraging future immigrants.

And Rwanda’s history of negotiating deals of this kind makes it easier to work with, said Alberto‑Horst Neidhardt, head of the migration program at the European Policy Center, a think tank.

“It meets some of the basic criteria,” he said. “Plus, there’s a precedent, so the taboo has been broken.”

Of course, attempts to put migrant centers in third countries have run into roadblocks. The British plan involving Rwanda did not compulsorily deport anyone, and cost Britain nearly $1 billion before it tanked.

Supporters say the new five-country program will meet a need.

“They don’t have a legal ground to to be here,” Morten Bodskov, Denmark’s minister for immigration and integration, told reporters last month, speaking of the migrants being targeted. “The return hub model is an answer to that.”

The European Union has indicated that the program has the bloc’s support.

The project has come after “careful preparatory work, including with regard to ensuring the respect for human rights,” Markus Lammert, a spokesman for the E.U. executive, said on Monday.

item.title: Pope Leo, Weeks After Surgery, Holds Up Well on South America Trip
item.description:
Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.

They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.

Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?

“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”

It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.

The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

Despite the journalists’ midair concerns, the pope showed no visible difficulty as he descended the staircase in Lima onto a red carpet to greet Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and accept flowers from two children. Videos soon emerged showing what Leo did during the flight instead of taking questions from reporters: He visited the cockpit and talked to the air traffic control tower.

Throughout the trip, Leo has appeared robust and confident. He has walked up and down stairs, rode around — often standing — in his popemobile, blessed babies (including some dressed to look like him), leaned down to hug people in wheelchairs, sang along with hymns and local anthems, and spoken in a strong voice during his homilies and speeches.

At a vigil for youth at a stadium in Lima, he caught a rosary a young woman threw at him as he passed in the popemobile, and then effortlessly tossed it back. He has seemed equally adroit mentally. At one point in Peru, his home for years, he accidentally started a speech in Italian, then quickly switched to Spanish, laughing and apologizing. “Here, at home, and I’m speaking Italian!” he said.

The pope has visited presidential palaces and impoverished neighborhoods, met with students and visited a prison, as well as facilities for older citizens and the disabled.

Over the weekend, he traveled by helicopter to a remote town in the Andes to celebrate Mass. On Sunday alone, he flew from Chiclayo to Cusco, a Peruvian city more than 11,000 feet above sea level. There he gave a prayer and blessing before flying again to Pucallpa, a city in the rainforest, roughly 500 feet above sea level where he watched dances by Amazonian performers.

By the time Leo led Mass in a sports field there, he looked a little sapped — but then so did those of us in the traveling press corps.

When he spoke in Cusco, his voice was clear, and he showed no hint of altitude sickness as rain pounded down around the covered platform where he stood. In the city’s central square, Plaza de Armas, the pope dedicated a prayer to those who “are suffering in body and soul because of illness.” He did not mention his own recent brush with disease.

Before the pope arrived in the square, Vanessa Loagca, 39, said she understood that “this trip is a big sacrifice for the pope’s health.” Along with her husband and two children, Ms. Loagca had slept overnight in the square to secure a spot at the front for a good view of the pope. “We feel a lot of love for him,” she said.

Lung specialists said the pope’s stamina fell within a normal range but was still notable.

“Most patients that I know wouldn’t be so active this soon after surgery,” said Dr. Natalie Liu, a thoracic surgeon and oncologist at Stanford University Hospital. “But I also feel like he probably has a lot of incentive and purpose in his life.”

The trip to Peru, in particular, has been significant for Leo, who served there for 20 years as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a Peruvian citizen. He is “going back home, honoring his country, feeling the love from his people,” said Prof. Christopher D. Tirres, an expert on Latin America at Santa Clara University.

On occasion, Leo has noted the concerns about his health. On the flight from Rome to Montevideo, Uruguay, the first stop on the trip, the pope told reporters that he knew some people wondered if he would be able to travel so soon after surgery. “From the first day I had no doubt, and was convinced that this trip had to go forward,” he said.

And in Lima, speaking to a group of bishops, priests and nuns at a prayer service at a cathedral, he took a gibe at the “doubting Thomases” who had predicted that he would postpone the journey. “But God is great and his grace is bigger than all of us, and I’m very happy to be here with you,” he said.

Some of the faithful said they feared the pope might be overextending himself.

“His condition was delicate,” said Donaldo Rodríguez, 60, at the Mass outside Chiclayo. “He’s come out because he has a commitment to the Lord to serve the people, but I don’t think he should have come. He needs to take care of himself. He really ought to be resting after all this.”

With modern surgical techniques, most patients “are back to their base line” within two to four weeks after the procedure, said Dr. Zaid Abdelsattar, a thoracic surgeon at Loyola Medicine in Chicago. Dr. Abdelsattar said that while some fatigue could be expected, patients “can live their life to the fullest, just like they have been before.” That is particularly the case if they were otherwise healthy before the surgery and the cancer was caught early, as was the case with Leo, he said.

Even if the pope appears to have recovered from his health scare, he will face regular screenings for the next five years. “There is still a chance that the lung cancer can come back,” said Dr. Abdelsattar.

For many, Leo’s presence was an inspiration.

Francisco de la Cruz Barrera, 67, whose leg was amputated after a motorcycle accident, was pushed in a wheelchair to attend the pope’s Mass near Chiclayo. Mr. de la Cruz said it was important for him to be there because he believed God had given him another chance after his crash.

Leo, Mr. de la Cruz said, “seems quite strong.” But given the pope’s recent illness, he said, “We must continue to pray for him.”

Mitra Taj contributed reporting from Chiclayo, Peru.

item.title: 10 Numbers That Might Change How You See Asia
item.description:
President Trump’s trip to Asia this week will be largely be seen as a test of American power in the main region where the United States and China compete for influence.

His meetings in Manila and Shenzhen, China, will be scrutinized for shifts on trade and security. Deals he might strike with Beijing — plus a gathering with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia — will put the world’s great-power contest on display, as all three seek to show strength.

But Asia is not just a theater of competition. Many countries in the region have become wealthier, more technologically advanced and increasingly interconnected. Especially now, as China’s military becomes more threatening and the United States less reliable, they are hedging against greatness and relying more on neighbors.

Asian students and workers are moving to neighboring states. Countries with expanding defense industries are selling weapons to new partners. Nations that compete for high-tech investment are even making plans to cooperate on energy and cybersecurity.

“They’re all looking at what more they can do together when the great powers are behaving so badly,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam and adjunct professor of geopolitics at Fulbright University in Ho Chi Minh City. “If you’re a middle power, you’re thinking ‘I need more options’.”

Here are a few numbers that provide a sense of what the region contributes to the global economy, and how its nations are becoming more bound together to shape the world.

The population of the 11 nations that make up the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a regional grouping that is holding its annual summit in Manila. ASEAN approved a digital framework agreement on Saturday that aims to create a multilateral digital market. If it rolls out smoothly next year, a small business in Vietnam could sell and ship products to Singapore with invoices, payment and customs handled through a regional online system.

The value of the Asia-Pacific market for medical tourism — the world’s largest. With portable insurance and medical visas, it’s becoming common to travel for better or more affordable cancer care, orthopedics, dentistry or cosmetic surgery. Life expectancy in high-income countries (like Japan) is around 84, compared with 79.8 in the United States, where health care costs are roughly twice as high.

The share of the world’s semiconductor chips that are manufactured in Asia. Without China, about 55 to 60 percent are made in Asia, led by South Korea and Taiwan, which makes more than 90 percent of the world’s high-end chips. The global market is worth roughly $1.5 trillion.

The number of top-grossing musical acts in Asia that were K-pop performers from August 2025 to July 2026. The top four earners for live shows in Asia were all K-pop stars, with Seventeen topping the list. Lady Gaga ranked fifth in the region.

The number of universities in the Asia-Pacific region in the QS global top 100. Among them are 11 in mainland China and Hong Kong, plus nine in Australia. There are 37 in Europe and 26 in the United States.

The number of airline passenger journeys across the Asia-Pacific, excluding China, in 2024. Driven by booming demand in India and Southeast Asia, regional traffic is projected to more than double to 4.1 billion passengers over the next two decades.

The approximate cost of Indonesia’s recent deal to buy India’s BrahMos supersonic missile systems for coastal defense. India has inked similar deals with Vietnam and the Philippines, as the region seeks alternatives to expensive Western weapons systems.

The total number of Uniqlo stores worldwide, up from 1,795 in 2016. Even as its retail footprint in China has declined, growth in Southeast Asia, India and Australia has continued. The Japanese fashion brand is now one of the world’s fastest growing clothing retailers.

The number of Japanese visits to South Korea in 2025 — a record for two countries that have been gradually overcoming a long history of resentment. The curiosity goes both ways: Koreans also set a record for trips to Japan last year, with 9.46 million visits.

The number of cross-border energy projects planned among ASEAN countries. With high-voltage lines on land and plans for some of the longest power cables ever to be placed underwater, the goal is to more than double transmission capacity and to pave the way for a multilateral power market that is more reliant on renewable energy, like hydropower.

item.title: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
item.description:
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.

Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.

Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.

“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”

In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.

His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

Placing sophisticated and sprawling military sites near the continuous water and power supply provided by dams would be logical, said seven water and military experts interviewed by The New York Times.

This gives Tehran “operational continuity,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former longtime Iran analyst for Israel’s military intelligence agency.

“Iran has a strong incentive to ensure that its missile complexes are not dependent on the broader national infrastructure for essential services,” Mr. Citrinowicz said. He added that it was reasonable to assess “that Iran has invested in some degree of autonomous or redundant infrastructure,” like dams and water projects, for its missile facilities.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Energy, which is partly responsible for dam construction, did not respond to requests for comment. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, which also plays a role in dam construction, did not respond to a request either.

Iran calls the subterranean sites its “missile cities” — heavily fortified tunnels and rooms dug deep beneath the mountains, used not only to store and deploy long-range ballistic missiles and drones, but also to produce them.

Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with the Washington Institute and an expert on Iranian military affairs, estimates that there are at least 30 missile sites across the country. Very few countries maintain as elaborate a system of underground military sites as Iran, he said, citing North Korea as an exception.

As a country that often experiences water shortages, Iran still does need dams. “Many dams in Iran serve essential civilian purposes, including water supply, irrigation and hydropower generation, particularly in a water-scarce country. Any potential military role should not overshadow these functions,” Dr. Shokri said.

By highlighting the extent and location of concealed missile sites in remote parts of the country, the U.S. and Israeli airstrikes may also have shed light on another puzzle that has troubled environmentalists: What are the reasons behind a string of arrests in 2018 of wildlife conservationists working in protected areas?

The Revolutionary Guards, whose intelligence arm carried out the arrests, did not comment about them for this article, and a definitive explanation remains elusive. But some environmentalists said they now suspect that the conservation workers may have accidentally happened upon sensitive military sites.

In 2018, the intelligence wing of the Revolutionary Guards detained dozens of conservationists on charges of espionage. One of them, Kavous Seyed-Emami, a founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, died in state custody. Several other members of the group, who spent years in prison, said they were tortured and sexually harassed.

At the time, senior Iranian officials said they were unaware of the allegations of mistreatment and that they would be examined.

Iranian authorities accused the conservationists of using cameras — intended for monitoring the habitats of rare and endangered species like the Asiatic cheetah — to instead gather intelligence for the United States and Israel.

“One of the accusations leveled against me was that I had trained lizards to spy on military installations,” said Morad Tahbaz, a founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, who spent more than five years in prison.

Political analysts suspected an effort by the Revolutionary Guards to undermine the reformist government in power at the time, which was trying to open the country to investment and expertise in various sectors including the environment.

“I think it is possible that the Guards saw anyone doing fieldwork near these sites, even wildlife conservationists, as a potential security threat,” said Nik Kowsar, a prominent Iranian environmental and water analyst in exile in Washington.

Kaveh Madani, who was deputy head of Iran’s department of environment when he was arrested in the 2018 crackdown, said that conservation groups never worked in wilderness areas without permission from the government and intelligence services.

The targeting of two Iranian regions in recent airstrikes provides intriguing examples.

Amir Aghakouchak, a prominent water expert at the University of California, Irvine, had long been perplexed by the construction of a massive project to transfer water from the mountainous Zagros region to central Yazd.

Airstrikes in March on the Yazd region prompted reports, including in The Financial Times, of a major missile facility in the area. Mr. Aghakouchak said he began to suspect that the water project “may have been influenced, at least in part, by military considerations.”

Mr. Tahbaz, of the wildlife heritage foundation, said he was always mystified, during his time in prison, by his interrogators’ fixation on his team’s work in Hormozgan Province, where there was a project to support the rare Laristan wild sheep. “They were incredibly sensitive about that area,” he recalled.

On July 14, U.S. airstrikes hit the Tarom Protected Area in Hormozgan, killing the family of a local wildlife ranger in the process. The U.S. military said it was targeting military infrastructure and coastal defenses. Mr. Nadimi, the military expert, said the location was not far from where military analysts believe Iran constructed a missile base deep below ground.

Environmentalists knew the area for something entirely different.

“It had a storage shed with hay,” Mr. Kowsar said, “for Laristan wild sheep.”

item.title: Austria Looks to Strip Citizenship of Ex-Minister Who Moved to Russia
item.description:
The Austrian authorities have taken initial steps to revoke the citizenship of a former foreign minister who moved to Russia — a country she has lauded for its “genuine freedom” — and who has repeatedly denigrated Austria while echoing Kremlin-friendly talking points.

Karin Kneissl made international headlines when she danced with President Vladimir Putin of Russia at her wedding in 2018, when she was her nation’s top diplomat.

Since then, she has angered many of her compatriots with regular barbs against her country of birth and its citizens.

That the Austrian state would even consider the extraordinary step of revoking her citizenship reflects a national weariness about the former foreign minister. It follows a prolonged national debate over whether Ms. Kneissl retained the right to remain Austrian after — both physically and by all appearances ideologically — turning her back on her homeland.

Ms. Kneissl, who served as foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, made her very public move to Russia in 2023, a year after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She was hired to run a think tank in St. Petersburg.

Over the years, Ms. Kneissl, 61, seems to have taken pleasure in denigrating Austrians in interviews with Russian-friendly media. Earlier this year, for example, she repeated her claim that Hitler, who was born in Austria, was typically Austrian. She also said that her countrymen had acted like hyenas toward her.

Such comments served to bolster a push to strip her of her citizenship. The initiative has been led by the liberal party NEOS, which is run by the current foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger.

“Why does Kneissl continue to appear prominently as Austria’s former foreign minister when she so obviously despises and hates our country?” Yannick Shetty, a NEOS member of the Austrian Parliament, asked in January in response to Ms. Kneissl’s remarks.

On Monday, officials in Vienna confirmed that an inquiry into the former minister had been launched. They said they were looking at whether she had obtained a second citizenship and whether her conduct significantly harmed “the interests or reputation of the Republic.”

It remains unclear if the inquiry will actually lead to the revocation of her citizenship and, if so, how long it might take.

Ms. Kneissl was proposed for the post of foreign minister in 2017 by the far-right Freedom Party of Austria, though she was never a member of that party.

After leaving Austria in 2020, she went to France and Lebanon before moving to a little village southeast of Moscow in the heartland of Russia.

On Monday, Ms. Kneissl said she knew that steps were being taken to revoke her citizenship. In comments reported by the Russian state news agency Tass, she said that if Austria moved forward with the plan, she would end up stateless and need to apply for travel documents from the United Nations.
